title: Hard carbon is quietly deciding how far sodium-ion can go
subtitle: The cathode gets the headlines. The anode sets the ceiling.
summary: Sodium-ion cells are cheap on paper. Whether they are cheap in practice depends on a material most cost models still treat as a rounding error.

seo.title: Hard carbon and the real limit on sodium-ion batteries
seo.description: Why anode design, not cathode chemistry, may decide whether sodium-ion cells hit their cost targets.

blocks.text: Sodium sits directly below lithium in the periodic table, and for a decade that similarity carried the field's optimism. Sodium is abundant, evenly distributed, and cheap. The cathodes work. What has proved harder is the other electrode.

Graphite, which stores lithium comfortably between its layers, barely accepts sodium at all. The working substitute is hard carbon: a disordered, non-graphitising carbon full of curved layers, pores and defects, made by pyrolysing anything from petroleum pitch to coconut shell.

Reversible capacity in hard carbon comes from two mechanisms that respond differently to processing. Sloping-region storage is adsorption at defects and edges; the low-voltage plateau is filling of closed nanopores. Push the pyrolysis temperature up and the plateau grows while the slope shrinks.

blocks.caption: Schematic of sodium storage in a disordered carbon: surface adsorption on the sloping region, pore filling on the plateau.

blocks.text: The trade-off is first-cycle efficiency. Every square metre of accessible surface consumes sodium building an interphase, and that sodium comes out of the cathode. Below roughly 85 per cent first-cycle efficiency, the cell needs excess cathode, and the cost advantage over lithium iron phosphate starts to erode.

Cost models for sodium-ion typically vary cathode chemistry and hold the anode fixed. That is backwards. Cathode raw material is where the theoretical saving sits, but anode yield, tap density and first-cycle loss are where the saving is spent.

Two directions look promising: pre-sodiation additives that pay the interphase cost from the cathode side without oversizing it, and precursor selection aimed at closed porosity rather than surface area. Biomass precursors are attractive on cost and carbon accounting, less so on batch consistency.

items: Stevens, D. A. & Dahn, J. R. High capacity anode materials for rechargeable sodium-ion batteries. J. Electrochem. Soc. 147, 1271 (2000).
Bommier, C. et al. Predicting capacity of hard carbon anodes in sodium-ion batteries. Nano Lett. 15, 5888 (2015).
